# Brief: assemble the readiness review for the October shutdown

We have eleven days of shutdown booked in October and four workstreams that have
never been sequenced against each other. Last year two of them collided on day
six, the drive train work waited two days on a crew that was committed
elsewhere, and we handed back a line that had to be opened again in November.
I am not willing to run that again on a verbal plan.

Your job is to produce the readiness review document we will take into the
pre-shutdown meeting. It has to cover all four workstreams, it has to say what
each one needs from the others and when, and for each one it has to name the
acceptance test we will use to call that workstream finished. Where we have
written something down before about how one of these jobs goes wrong, find it
and use it rather than re-deriving it, because most of what went wrong last year
was something one of us already knew.

## Workstream one: the drive train

Two gearboxes come out and go to the rebuild vendor on day one and come back on
day seven. That is the long pole and everything else is scheduled around it.

The part I want the review to be explicit about is what we do when they come
back. We accepted the last two rebuilds on a ten-minute run on the stand and a
signature, and both of them developed excessive play at the output inside a
month of going back into service. When the first one was stripped here the
finding was in the stack of shims behind the bearing carrier — it had been put
back to the dimension it came apart at rather than the dimension the new
bearings actually wanted, and a difference that small is quiet on a stand and
opens up under load in a few weeks.

I want the acceptance test written so that it measures that, and I want it
measured cold, before the unit has been run, because a warm housing reads
differently and the last measurement we took was taken after twenty minutes of
running and told us nothing.

There is also a standing argument on the floor that this complaint is really
about chain tension, because tension is the thing you can reach without opening
anything and adjusting it does move the number you are measuring. The review
should say plainly whether that is the cause or a symptom, and it should say it
in a way that the fitters will accept, because I have lost this argument twice
by asserting it.

## Workstream two: the vessel and its joints

The vessel comes off on day two, goes to the shop for internal inspection, and
goes back on day nine. Reassembly is the piece I am most worried about, because
we did it in a hurry last year and we had a weeping joint on the sealing face
within a fortnight of handing back.

The crew that did it is not the crew that will do it this time, so whatever we
know about how those fasteners go back has to be in the document rather than in
somebody's head. My recollection is that there is a defined order and a defined
number of passes, and that going straight to the final value in one pass is the
specific thing that distorts the face and produces exactly the leak we had. I
would like that stated with the reason attached, because a procedure that says
"three passes" without saying why gets compressed to one pass by a crew that is
running late on day nine, and day nine is precisely when they will be running
late.

The acceptance test here is a pressure hold. Say how long, say at what value,
and say who signs it.

## Workstream three: the turbine rotor

We are swapping the rotor for the refurbished spare. This is a straight swap on
paper and I do not believe it is a straight swap in practice.

The specific worry is the balancing. The spare has been sitting for two years
and it was balanced before it went into storage, and the records we have are
filed against the machine it came out of rather than against the rotor itself.
If those weights describe the housing and not the rotor then fitting the spare
into this housing will bring somebody else's imbalance with it, and we will find
out about it on the vibration trend two weeks after handback, which is the worst
possible time to find out about it.

So the review needs to say where the balancing record for a rotor is supposed to
live, whether the record we are holding is the right kind of record, and what we
do on the day if it turns out not to be. I would rather spend half a day on the
balancing machine during the shutdown than three days on a running machine in
November.

## Workstream four: closing the books on the job

This one is not mechanical and it is on the list because it went wrong last year
in a way that cost us more argument than any of the mechanical work.

The shutdown is capitalised as a single job and the job has to be closed in the
month it finishes. Last year the contractor invoices for the final three days
arrived after the period had been closed, and bringing them in afterwards took
an adjustment, and the adjustment lost the line-by-line trace back to the work
order. The finance side is still asking questions about it and I cannot answer
them, because the detail that would answer them is what the adjustment
flattened.

What I want in the review is the cut-off. Say the date by which every
contractor's final numbers have to be with us, say what we check them against
before anything closes, and say explicitly that the checking happens before the
close and not after it. If there is a note somewhere about why the order of
those two matters, quote it, because "we should do it in this order" is an
instruction people reorder under time pressure and "doing it in the other order
costs you the audit line" is not.

## What the document has to look like

One page per workstream, in the order above, and then a single sequencing page
at the front that puts the eleven days on one axis and the four workstreams on
the other, with the dependencies marked. Every workstream page ends with its
acceptance test and the name of the person who signs it.

Two things I do not want. I do not want a risk register with probability and
impact columns; we have never once acted on one. And I do not want the review to
tell me that a workstream is fine because it went fine the last time it went
fine — three of these four have a specific failure in the recent past and I want
each of those failures named on its page.

## What I already have

The shutdown dates are fixed and booked. The rebuild vendor has confirmed the
seven-day turnaround in writing. The vessel inspection scope is agreed with the
inspector. The rotor is in the store and has been turned monthly. The contractor
list is the same four firms as last year and their rates are agreed.

What I do not have is any of it written down in one place, and I do not have the
sequencing, and I do not have the acceptance tests. That is what I am asking you
for.

Take as long as you need on the detail and come back with something we can put
in front of eight people who will each read only their own page.
